turns.prompt_text: I like to put a small garden bed in my ground floor apartment on the exterior after the patio. I could do it on the patio or I could do it in the grass. I would prefer to do in the grass would get sunlight. How should I go about asking them
turns.response_html:
Putting a garden bed in the common grass area is a great idea for getting that prime sunlight, but since it's technically shared or managed property, you’ll definitely want to get written approval first. Property managers are usually protective of the grass because of landscaping crews, lawnmowers, and future tenant turnover.

To give yourself the absolute best chance of getting a "yes," you want to approach them with a clear, low-risk plan rather than a vague question. Landlords love things that are temporary, neat, and won't cost them money to fix later.

Here is a step-by-step strategy and a template you can adapt to email your property manager.

Strategy for a "Yes"

  • Pitch a Raised Bed, Not Digging: Do not ask to dig up the turf. Property managers will almost always say no to that because it ruins the lawn permanently. Instead, pitch a contained, raised garden bed or a series of neat planter boxes that sit on top of the ground.
  • Address the Lawnmower Dilemma: The biggest concern for the maintenance crew is mowing. If your bed is out in the grass, it becomes an obstacle. Assure them that you will keep the perimeter clean and that it won't interfere with their route, or offer to weed-wack around it yourself.
  • Emphasize Restorability: Explicitly state that when your lease ends, you will remove the bed and restore the grass (a quick throw of some grass seed), leaving no permanent changes.

Email Template

You can adapt this template to send to your leasing office or property manager. It's polite, professional, and addresses their structural concerns before they even have to ask.

Subject: Request for minor patio-adjacent garden placement - Apartment [Your Apt Number]

Dear [Property Manager Name or Leasing Team],

I hope your week is going well.

I am writing to request permission to set up a small, temporary raised garden bed just past my patio edge in the grass area to catch the direct sunlight.

I want to ensure this doesn't cause any inconvenience for the maintenance or landscaping teams, so I’ve planned it with the following guidelines:

  • No Digging: The bed will be entirely self-contained and sit on top of the ground, so no turf will be dug up or altered.
  • Maintenance-Friendly: I will ensure it is placed neatly right against the patio transition so it doesn't obstruct the lawnmowers, and I will personally maintain the immediate perimeter so the landscaping crew doesn't have extra work.
  • Fully Restorable: This is completely temporary. When my lease is up, I will remove the structure and restore the grass underneath.

I've attached a quick sketch/photo of the intended spot just to show the scale. Please let me know if this would be acceptable or if there are specific guidelines I need to follow.

Thank you for your time and help!

Best regards,

[Your Name]
[Your Phone Number]
[Your Apartment Number]

The Backup Plan

If they come back with a hard "no" on placing anything in the grass due to HOA rules or mowing contracts, don't sweat it. You can instantly pivot to a high-yield patio setup.

You can use rolling planter boxes or vertical garden towers right on the edge of your patio concrete. If you push them right up to the boundary line, you can usually catch almost the exact same sunlight profile without touching a single blade of corporate grass.
